newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian rail will compensate travellers for chaos.
newsitem.headline: Italian rail will compensate travellers for chaos.

text.p: Italian state railways (FS) promised on Tuesday to compensate passengers following a weekend of travel chaos, but attacks on the government's transport policy grew after another rail accident on Monday claimed three lives.

In an advertisement in Italy's major dailies, FS promised to mail a free ticket to everyone who proved they had travelled by train through Rome and Naples over the weekend, when rail travel was brought to a standstill by a derailment and a crane crash.
"FS apologizes to its clients for the enormous disruption," the full-page ad said.

The weekend's woes were compounded on Monday night, when an express train slammed into a car on a level crossing near Rome, instantly killing two people, including a pregnant woman, who were travelling in the car.
A third person died later in hospital.

News reports said on Tuesday the level-crossing accident may have been caused by an overload of traffic on the route that spilled over from the havoc of the weekend -- one of the busiest of the year as thousands of Italians began their August breaks.
"Black August for the Railroads," was the main headline on more than one major Italian daily on Tuesday.

"This is what happens when plans and projects are concerned only with balance sheets and do not place at the centre of attention the interest of and respect for people," railed the Vatican newspaper, Osservatore Romano.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi, Transport Minister Claudio Burlando and FS president Giancarlo Cimoli, all under attack over the accidents, held an emergency meeting on Tuesday.

The chaos began when a train jumped the tracks in Rome on Saturday, injuring four passengers, and then a crane working to remove it collapsed on Sunday, blocking the main links which connect north and south Italy, effectively slicing the national rail network in half.

Tens of thousands of travellers passing through the Italian capital were crammed onto buses which ferried them between trains on either side of the divide. Some were stranded at stations for up to 12 hours.
"This chain reaction of accidents is a serious clue...to the uncertain and precarious structures that dangerously hold up Italy," said an editorial in Turin's daily La Stampa on Tuesday.
"More importantly it shows the dramatic lack of attention given by authorities and railway officials."
The far-right National Alliance has said it will call a vote of no-confidence in Burlando when parliament reopens in September.
"Prodi, Burlando and their party are directly responsible for these disasters. They have to own up to their political and personal responsibilities," AN official Maurizio Gasparri said.

Burlando said on Monday it would take five years for Italy's archaic railways to reach the technological levels seen in other European countries, and that the government planned to invest some 42 trillion lire ($23 billion) in the network.
